🐛 Describe the bug
test_python_reference_consistency appears to assume that the numerics of CPU and CUDA are implemented equivalently. This is not true and leads to a lot of tolerance overrides that have to be manually entered whenever CPU is computing in, e.g., bfloat16, while CUDA is computing in float. test_decomps.py strategy is to compute the "true" result (via double) and then accept whenever the decomp is closer than the ATen implementation. We should do it this way.
Alternately, we can stop testing reference consistency on non-CUDA backends
cc @mruberry @ezyang @ngimel @Chillee
Versions
master

Issue description
In the example below, assigning a parameter to tensor doesn't seem to pass gradient information, unless a list is used for indexing.
Code example
import torch
torch.__version__  # '1.11.0'
z = torch.zeros(3, 2)

z[:, 0] = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0))
z

# tensor([[1., 0.],
#         [1., 0.],
#         [1., 0.]])  # <------------

z[:, [0]] = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0))
z

# tensor([[1., 0.],
#         [1., 0.],
#         [1., 0.]], grad_fn=<CopySlices>)  # <------------
... is this behaviour expected?

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Running training on 2 different machines for various experiments with T5, 3B and 150K dataset. EC2, A100, PyTorch Nightly 514.
Training crashes with hang after completing training step for epoch 6 or 7.
Of note - if you look at the saving info, you'll see that rank 0 fails to complete it's save in all these cases before the timeout is hit, meaning that may be what is causing the timeout (?).



At the end of training (training is done for that epoch, moving into validation loop) after epoch 6+, receive notice about :
[E ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp:737] [Rank 3] Watchdog caught collective operation timeout: WorkNCCL(SeqNum=3738254, OpType=_ALLGATHER_BASE, Timeout(ms)=1800000) ran for 1809440 milliseconds before timing out.
[E ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp:737] [Rank 0] Watchdog caught collective operation timeout: WorkNCCL(SeqNum=3738254, OpType=REDUCE, Timeout(ms)=1800000) ran for 1809061 milliseconds before timing out.

class MyIterableDataset(torch.utils.data.IterableDataset):
    def __init__(self, start, end):
        super(MyIterableDataset).__init__()
        assert end > start, "this example code only works with end >= start"
        self.start = start
        self.end = end

    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(range(self.start, self.end))


# Define a `worker_init_fn` that configures each dataset copy differently
def worker_init_fn(worker_id):
    worker_info = torch.utils.data.get_worker_info()
    dataset = worker_info.dataset  # the dataset copy in this worker process
    overall_start = dataset.start
    overall_end = dataset.end
    # configure the dataset to only process the split workload
    per_worker = int(math.ceil((overall_end - overall_start) / float(worker_info.num_workers)))
    worker_id = worker_info.id
    dataset.start = overall_start + worker_id * per_worker
    dataset.end = min(dataset.start + per_worker, overall_end)


if __name__ == '__main__':

📚 The doc issue
While the current PyTorch source code often contains type hints for signatures of public functions, the type hint information is missing from the generated documentation.
For example, compare https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.relu.html with the linked source at https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/_modules/torch/nn/functional.html#relu
In the source, the signature of relu is clearly presented and input is clearly indicated to be a Tensor: def relu(input: Tensor, inplace: bool = False) -> Tensor:
In the documentation, there is no type information at all and it is not obvious what type input needs to be: torch.nn.functional.relu(input, inplace=False) → Tensor
Thus, a simple reading of the documentation alone does not clarify the expected type of the function arguments.
If API documentation contains type information derived from the type hints in the source code, it will be more useful and understandable to readers without requiring them to examine the source code.
While in some cases there could be an implicit convention regarding function arguments of certain groups of functions, I don't think those conventions are documented clearly in one obvious and accessible document, so explicit type information in the actual API documentation of each function or class will be useful especially to new users of PyTorch.
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
Modify/configure the sphinx documentation generation to automatically include type information in the generated documentation based on the type hints present in the source code. Remove manually-produced redundant documentation from the source code docstrings like the relu(input, inplace=False) -> Tensor above when automatic documentation generation includes relevant type hint information.

Overview
PR #77356 introduce sharded_state_dict that return a state dict that contains the unflattened, sharded parameters. Current implementation requires to do all gather over each unflattened, sharded parameters when loading the state dict. This may cause some performance bottleneck for large models.
Possible Solution
Instead of doing allgather over each unflattened parameter, we can concat the local shards of all the parameters in one FSDP module and perform only one allgather per FSDP module.

print(list(offline_bn_torch.buffers())[1])

print(np.std(inputs_2d, axis=0)**2)
print(torch.var(torch.tensor(inputs_2d), 0, unbiased=True, keepdim=False))
print(torch.var(torch.tensor(inputs_2d), 0, unbiased=False, keepdim=False))
